newsitem.title: FRANCE: Small shifts produce huge swings in French polls.
newsitem.headline: Small shifts produce huge swings in French polls.

text.p: French opinion pollsters came under scrutiny on Monday after two polls on this month's parliamentary election showed a big swing in seats to the ruling centre-right coalition based on only a small shift in voting intentions.

Surveys by the SOFRES and IFOP institutes both projected a majority of at least 130 seats for President Jacques Chirac's conservative alliance, just a week after the same firms had given the centre-right only a slight lead.
Polls by other firms taken in the middle of last week had suggested a neck-and-neck race with the coalition's majority of seats down in single figures.
So who, if anyone, is wrong, or is it just an indication of yoyo behaviour by fickle voters in a particularly dull campaign?

The SOFRES survey, taken on Friday and Saturday, put the coalition about 150 seats ahead of the left in the 577-seat National Assembly even though it found a combined left vote of 41.5 percent compared to 39.9 for the centre-right.

Pollsters defended the scientific basis of the projections, saying they showed how volatile the electorate still was and how France's two-round voting system in single-member constituencies amplifies the victory of the biggest party.
"The voting system is so sensitive that a one-point shift towards either of the main blocs makes an enormous diffence in the number of seats," said Carine Marce of SOFRES' political department.

France's six big polling institutes have a fairly good track record for measuring the popular vote in past elections, although they acknowledge it is much more difficult to translate it accurately before the first round into seats won in runoffs.

By law, no polls may be published in the last week before the first ballot, or between the two rounds, although polling firms continue to work intensively for the parties and private clients, and some are usually published in foreign countries, circumventing the French ban.

Published polls before the 1995 French presidential election all put the eventual winner, Jacques Chirac, ahead on the first round, but it was Socialist candidate Lionel Jospin who came out top of the first-ballot vote.
Red-faced pollsters claimed there had been a late swing to Jospin after the pre-election poll-publishing blackout.

The SOFRES poll in Monday's Le Figaro daily showed a one-point drop in the Socialist vote to 27 percent compared to a poll a week earlier, while the ruling RPR-UDF alliance gained a point to stand at 35 percent, with "other right" allied candidates down half a point at 4.5 percent.
The Communists were stable on 10 and the extreme left on two percent, while miscellaneous "other left" candidates were half a point up at 2.5 percent.
The extreme-right National Front was one point down on 14 percent and the ecologists steady at five percent.
"The main differences are the slight gain for the coalition and the fact that more National Front voters say they will vote for the mainstream right on the second round," Marce said.
She said one factor which pollsters usually did not publish -- the likely turnout -- could cause wide discrepancies.
On a low turnout, the National Front would need a higher share of votes cast to win the 12.5 percent of registered voters necessary to contest the runoff.

IFOP's poll, taken on Friday for the Journal du Dimanche, showed a bigger shift in voting intentions. It gave the combined right 41 percent (up three percent in a week) to 38.5 percent for the combined left (down 2.5 percent in a week), 13.5 percent for the National Front (down 0.5 percent) and seven percent for ecologists.
